_meta.directives: Fiche recentrée sur le nom (2026-10-03), passe de correction : chaque piste d'origine est attribuée à qui la porte et citée à la page dans les notes de sa source ; aucune n'est retenue comme la bonne. Ne pas étendre sans source dédiée.

oralTraditions.claim: The Mara belong to the same paternal branch as the Traoré: the two names share a common ancestor, Mansa Yurukara Nayni, and are of the same family as the Sako and the Kouyaté.
oralTraditions.carrier: Babou Condé, griot du village de Fadama, dans la préfecture de Kouroussa en Guinée
oralTraditions.collector: E. A. Bogacheva, lors d'entretiens menés en 2017
oralTraditions.context: Account reported in Russian in a university thesis

oralTraditions.claim: In the epic, two brothers, both Traoré, Oulamba the elder and Oulani the younger, bring back from the land of Do the young woman promised to the victor over the buffalo, and give her to the king of Manding, Naré Maghan Kon Fatta, before the birth of Soundiata. An editor's note records the tradition attached to it: when the younger brother has killed the buffalo, the elder composes a song in his honour on the spot, and the younger cries out, "Brother, if you were a griot, no one could resist you." From this sentence would come the separation between Traoré and Diabaté (Dioubaté) and the name Diabaté itself, and the Diabaté griots remain brothers of the Traoré. Another note derives from the same episode the joking kinship between Kondé and Traoré: the people of Do mocked the hunters who had preferred the ugly Sogolon to the beautiful girls.
oralTraditions.carrier: Djeli Mamadou Kouyaté, griot de Djeliba Koro, près de Siguiri
oralTraditions.collector: Djibril Tamsir Niane, qui l'a traduit en français
oralTraditions.context: Epic published in 1960; the separation of the two names is reported in the editor's notes

oralTraditions.claim: Tiramaghan Traoré, a general of Soundiata, is said to have defeated the king of Jolof and then conquered Casamance and Kaabu. The western Mandenka regard him as the founder of many kingdoms, including Kaabu, and the griots of Kaabu sing his deeds to the kora; he is given as the ancestor of the Traoré. The traditions do not agree on his end: several villages of Kaabu say they keep his remains, while traditions of Gangaran have him return to Mali.
oralTraditions.carrier: Les griots du Kaabu et les traditions du Gangaran
oralTraditions.collector: Le colloque sur les traditions orales du Kaabu de la Fondation Léopold-Sédar-Senghor, notamment M. Cissoko et Madina Ly-Tall, dont Djibril Tamsir Niane reprend les résultats
oralTraditions.context: Historical synthesis published by UNESCO in 1985; the link with the Traoré is given by a historian of the epic

oralTraditions.claim: Before the Mali empire, some of the Traoré live in the land of Kiri, but most inhabit the province later called Gangaran, north-west of Bouré. It is hunters of the Traoré clan who are said to have given the mother of Soundiata in marriage to King Maghan Kön Fatta.
oralTraditions.collector: Djibril Tamsir Niane et Youssouf Tata Cissé, d'après les écoles de tradition orale du Manding
oralTraditions.context: Historical synthesis published by UNESCO in 1985

writtenChronicles.claim: The name is said to come from a phrase, "À taá dá wéele", which the work does not translate and which it links to the call made to the ancestor. Túraman, a general in the time of Soundiata, had left the war in old age; when a war nearly cost Manden its existence, he was sent for, set out, defeated the enemies and brought back peace. The storytellers afterwards sang his descendants, recalling that their forebear had been called to that war, and they replied that without that call Manden was lost. Thus the lineage took the name Tárawele, and the ancestor's name, Túraman, became its jamu. The same work, written in N'ko by Souleymane Kanté, divides the Tárawele into four branches, Dàamasí, Nàyité, Sídimɛ and Jàbaatɛ́, and also reports that they are said to descend from Lònsanín; its author adds that he does not believe in an Arab origin.

linguisticReconstructions.claim: No dictionary consulted gives a meaning for the word: the dictionary of Mandinka clan names writes it Tàrawéle, with the variants Traore and Taraore, and defines it only as a clan name. Traoré is its French spelling.

One explanation concerns the ancestor's name, not the word Traoré: in Kaabu, where he is called Tiramagan or Siramagan, the name would be a title. Magan is an old word for "king", and sira the spear used in Kaabu, in an ordeal, to designate the person to be tested; Tiramagan would mean "chief of the ordeals", and an object of worship would have become a character. This is a hypothesis. In the Soundiata epic, Tiramagan is his general; in Kaabu, the founding narrative almost ignores this link.

The name has equivalents among other peoples: in Wolof country, a Traoré is received as a brother by the Diop and may take their name, and a Diop may become Traoré among the Mandenka. Tradition traces these correspondences between clan names back to the assembly held after Soundiata's victory, to whom events well after his time are also attributed; the practice continued after him.

For a foreigner, the jamu is the gateway into the social fabric: in Bamako, a Mandinka jamu is assigned to a newcomer to give them a place in the group. Today, the historical references of the pacts between names are often forgotten and people struggle to explain their origin.

casteOrSocialFunction.value: Status varies from one area to another; it is not an absence of status. Traoré is among the jamuw hɔrɔn, of free and non-artisan condition; the dictionary of jamuw records for the same entry hɔ́rɔn, then tontigi among the Bamana and the Maninka, then nùmu (blacksmith) among the Kagoro and the Wassoulounké. The numu side of the jamu is therefore attested, and the absence of a hereditary function does not hold for the whole area of the name.

sources.title: EthniAfrica — fiche du peuple Bambara, organisation clanique
sources.notes: Taken from the "Clan organisation" chapter of the fiche of the Bambara people.

sources.title: Soundjata ou l'épopée mandingue
sources.notes: Niane, Djibril Tamsir, Présence Africaine, 1960. Transcription of the narrative of the griot Djeli Mamadou Kouyaté of Djeliba Koro (Siguiri); it is the written record of an oral tradition. Pages read in the digitised copy on archive.org (SoundjataOuLepopeeMandingue), close to the printed edition without being identical to it: the two hunter brothers Oulamba and Oulani, from the land of Do (pp. 21-28); the note on the separation of the Traoré and the Diabaté and the origin of the name Diabaté, then the one on the joking kinship between Kondé and Traoré and its origin (p. 32). The narrative does not name Tiramaghan.

sources.title: Beyond the Mali Empire — A New Paradigm for the Sunjata Epic
sources.notes: Jansen, Jan, Universiteit Leiden; article published in The International Journal of African Historical Studies, cited from the author's version deposited at Leiden and its pagination. The author argues that the heroes of the Soundiata epic refer to ritual practices rather than to historical persons. Tiramagan is given as ancestor of the Traoré and founder of Kaabu in a narrative that almost ignores his link with Soundiata, and his name is read as "chief of the ordeals", a reading the author says was suggested to him by the historian Cornelia Giesing (p. 15).

sources.title: Bamadaba — dictionnaire des noms claniques (jamuw)
sources.notes: Annex of clan names of the Bamadaba, an electronic Bambara-French dictionary of the Corpus bambara de référence (Bailleul, Davydov, Erman, Maslinsky, Méric, Vydrin, 2011-2020, CC BY-NC-SA), pointed out by Vydrin in Mandenkan 63, 2020, pp. 89-110. Complete file consulted. The entry Tàrawéle gives the variants Traore and Taraore, the Bambara and Malinke groups, the statuses hɔ́rɔn, then tontigi among the Bamana and the Maninka, and nùmu (blacksmith) among the Kagoro and in Wassoulou, equivalents among other peoples (including Sane, Mane, Ouédraogo, Dembélé, Diouf, and Touré at Ségou), and as joking partners Jàra, Kɔ́nɛ, Jawara and Turɛ; it gives no meaning for the name. Joking ties are not always reciprocal from one entry to another: each pair is cited from the entry that carries it.

sources.title: A Guide to the Jembe
sources.notes: Charry, Eric, Percussive Notes 34(2), April 1996, pp. 66-72; the author is the ethnomusicologist of Mande Music (University of Chicago Press, 2000). A specialist journal article, not a peer-reviewed one: it is cited here for the attribution of jamuw to Mandinka social statuses (numu, jeli, horon), which it states by name, clan by clan, and not for the history of the jembe.

sources.title: Pouvoir, places et filiation : les senankuya au Mali
sources.notes: Canut, Cécile, Cahiers de praxématique, number 38, 2002, pp. 175-197. Field survey in Mali. It states what the pact requires: the relationship holds in perpetuity for all the descendants of the two lineages, marriage between them is prohibited (applied in varying degrees today, it specifies) and mutual aid is owed without reserve. Cited for the obligation itself; it does not name the pair of this fiche, which the entries cited alongside it carry.

sources.title: Pactes, alliances et plaisanteries. Pratiques locales, discours global
sources.notes: Canut, Cécile, and Smith, Étienne, Cahiers d'études africaines, number 184, 2006, p. 687 ff. Cited for the caution it carries: the idea that joking kinship soothes conflict is treated there as a hypothesis inherited from Radcliffe-Brown and taken up by conflict-resolution studies, hence as a discourse to be analysed and not as a measured effect. The first page is verified; the last page is not.

sources.title: Histoire générale de l'Afrique, IV : L'Afrique du XIIe au XVIe siècle — chapitre 6, Le Mali et la deuxième expansion manden
sources.notes: UNESCO, ed. D. T. Niane, 1985; chapter by D. T. Niane. Printed pages: according to the oral-tradition schools of Manding, some of the Traoré in the land of Kiri and most in the province later called Gangaran (p. 153); Mamadi Kani calling on the hunters of the Kamara, Keita, Konate and Traore clans, and the mother of Soundiata given in marriage by hunters of the Traore clan, according to Y. Cissé (p. 154); Tiramaghan Traore, general of Soundiata, founder of Kaabu according to the western Mandenka, his deeds sung by the griots of Kaabu, and the divergent traditions on his end (p. 157, note 41); a Traore received as a brother by the Diop in Wolof country and able to take their name (p. 158, note 44). The chapter gives no meaning for the name.

sources.title: Les noms de clan du Manden (jamu) dans les sources africaines, occidentales et arabes
sources.notes: Bogacheva, E. A., bachelor's thesis, Saint Petersburg State University, 2017, in Russian; supervised by A. Davydov, read over by V. Vydrin. Entry Tàrawéle, pp. 136-137: the forms Traore and Taraore and the statuses (p. 136); the joking partners and the origin recounted in Souleymane Kanté's N'ko work on the names and jamu of Manden, with the phrase "À taá dá wéele", the ancestor Túraman and the branches of the name (p. 137). Entry Mara: the narrative of the griot Babou Condé of Fadama, collected in 2017, on the common ancestor of the Mara and the Traoré (p. 104). Kanté's work, which deals mainly with Guinea, is read in the Russian translation given by the author of the thesis; the original N'ko text has not been read. A bachelor's thesis is not a peer-reviewed publication: it is cited for the testimonies it relays.

gaps.reason: Traoré and Tarawele are two spellings of one jamu, the first being the French spelling; the dictionary of jamuw adds a third, Taraore, under the same entry. It also lists Sane, Mane, Ouédraogo, Dembélé, Diouf and, at Ségou, Touré among its equivalences, clan names of other peoples held to be the same, an institution that the General History of Africa describes in its own way by noting that a Traoré settled in Wolof country may take the name Diop. Neither the spellings nor the equivalences make distinct lineages: none is treated as a homonym.
